query: Consider the following context: The ability to endure extreme corrosion in challenging environments is reduced in stainless steel. This can be addressed by appropriate surface modification techniques to redefine the surface with the required properties. In that context, which method can be used for improved corrosion resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A DFT-guided plasma oxidation treatment can be applied to stainless steel to form an engineered, dense, and adherent passivation oxide layer that substantially improves its resistance to extreme corrosive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Stainless steel with naturally forming, but inadequate, oxide layers that fail under extreme corrosive conditions.
generation.intervention: Application of a plasma oxidation process developed through DFT screening, which identifies and targets optimal passivation oxide phases for incorporation onto the surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to harsh, extreme corrosive environments such as high chloride concentrations, molten salts, or elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: A carefully tailored, uniform, and strongly adherent passivation oxide layer that acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
generation.mechanism: First‐principles simulations (DFT) predict oxide compositions that offer ideal adhesion and chemical inertness. Using these predictions, the plasma oxidation treatment deposits a nanostructured oxide film on the stainless steel surface, thereby redefining its surface properties without compromising the bulk material integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated stainless steel, the modified surface is expected to exhibit a significantly reduced corrosion rate under extreme conditions. While the degree of improvement is projected to be moderate to significant, the exact magnitude requires experimental validation.
generation.baseline: Untreated stainless steel relying on its naturally forming oxide layer that is not suited for extreme corrosive environments.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the treatment is anticipated under laboratory-simulated extreme conditions; variations in operational conditions (e.g., temperature, chemical composition of the corrosive medium) could influence the performance of the passivation layer.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal oxide composition and microstructure, as well as the scalability of the DFT-guided plasma oxidation process, remain uncertain and requiring further computational and experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of stainless steel samples: one group treated with the DFT-informed plasma oxidation process and a control group receiving no specialized surface treatment. Expose both groups to accelerated corrosion tests using a controlled extreme corrosive medium (e.g., a high chloride or molten salt environment) at elevated temperatures.
measurements: Corrosion rate via mass loss measurements
Surface morphology and coating integrity using SEM and AFM
Adhesion strength of the oxide layer through scratch testing
Chemical composition and phase verification using XPS and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DFT-guided plasma oxidation treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rates, improved oxide adhesion, and a stable passivation film compared to the untreated control samples, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6
